> 惠能一闻经语，心即开悟。

The sixth patriarch of Chan was a woodcutter who could not read.

He sold firewood to support his mother. One day a customer bought a load and told him to deliver it to a shop. He collected the money, stepped outside, and heard someone reciting a sutra. He listened to a line and something opened. He asked what the sutra was. The Diamond Sutra. He asked where the man had come from. Huangmei, where the Fifth Patriarch teaches, and he advises people to hold this sutra and see their own nature.

The man gave him ten taels of silver for his mother's upkeep and told him to go. He settled his mother, walked, and arrived in something over thirty days.

That is the whole of the first section's opening, and it is worth slowing down for, because the Platform Sutra begins with logistics: a wage, a mother, a walk of about a month. No light on the ground. No lotus.

## The test at the gate

The Fifth Patriarch asks where he is from and what he wants. He answers: a commoner from Xinzhou in Lingnan, come only to become a Buddha, nothing else.

The old man pushes: you are a southerner, and a *gelao* — a mountain barbarian. How could you become a Buddha?

The answer is the first doctrinal sentence in the book: *people may be northern or southern; Buddha-nature has no north or south. The barbarian's body differs from the master's, but what difference is there in Buddha-nature?*

Note what he does not say. He does not say the insult is unfair. He does not claim equal social standing. He separates two questions that the gatekeeper had fused: the body, which has a region, a surname, a rank, and the nature, which has none of those. The Fifth Patriarch's question was a trap set to see whether the boy would answer with the body or with the nature. He answered with the nature, and the old man immediately stopped talking and sent him to the back to split wood and pound rice — for eight months.

That reassignment reads like a rebuke and is actually a shelter. Later the patriarch explains it: *I thought your insight usable, but feared wicked people would harm you, so I said nothing to you.*

## Wiping a mirror, and having nowhere to put dust

Everyone knows the two verses. Fewer people notice that the first one is not wrong.

Shenxiu writes on the corridor wall: *The body is a bodhi tree, the mind a bright mirror stand; wipe it diligently at all times, let no dust alight.*

The book's judgment is precise: this verse builds something. A tree, a stand, a surface, and dust. It sets up a boundary between clean and dirty and assigns a labor to maintain it. At its own level it works — the patriarch tells the monks to recite it, says those who practice by it will not fall into evil paths. He also says its author has not entered the gate.

Huineng's reply removes the furniture: *Bodhi originally has no tree; the bright mirror has no stand. Originally there is not a single thing — where could dust alight?*

This is not a claim that nothing exists. It says the thing you were planning to wipe is not a thing. If there is no stand, dust has no address.

The distinction the commentary draws is between two postures: *he* — a constructed pairing of pure and impure, held by effort; and *he* in the sense of a whole that does not need the pairing in order to be itself. Shenxiu's practice is sincere and remains a construction. Huineng's verse is not a better mirror; it is the end of the mirror industry.

## 何期自性: five lines that describe, not define

That night, with a robe over the window so no one sees the lamp, the patriarch expounds the Diamond Sutra. When he reaches *one should produce a mind that abides nowhere*, the listener says: *how unexpected — the self-nature is originally pure; how unexpected — it is originally unborn and undying; how unexpected — it is originally complete in itself; how unexpected — it is originally unmoved; how unexpected — it can produce all things.*

Five sentences, all beginning the same way. *How unexpected* is a report of surprise, not a definition. Read them as five attributes of a substance and you have made the mistake the whole book is written against. The commentary is blunt about this: self-nature is not an independent, permanent entity situated somewhere inside the chest. It is the name emptiness takes when spoken from the side of a sentient being — said so that a person will turn around and look, not so that a person will install a new object of worship.

## Which one moved

Years later, at a temple, two monks argue about a banner in the wind. One says the wind moves. The other says the banner moves. The master says: *not the wind moving, not the banner moving — the benevolent one's mind moves.*

The cheap reading is that nothing moved, or that it is all in your head, which turns a public event into a private opinion. The banner is cloth; the wind is air in motion; at the level of conditions both statements are true and neither is the whole.

What he refuses is the shape of the question: pick one of the two as the cause. The commentary maps the pair onto its usual frame — banner as yin, having form; wind as yang, having force — and says the mind he points at is not a third item in the argument. It is what holds the pair without enlisting on either side.

## The test

Think of the last time you were certain who caused something — a delay, a slight, a failure. You had a culprit. Now ask: what did I need to be true about myself for that to be the answer?

That need is the dust. There is no stand for it. There never was.
